notes.front: A package holds a Division 1.3 explosive in compatibility group C. What goes in the asterisk space of its EXPLOSIVE label?
notes.back: A: The division number and compatibility group letter, 1.3C, on an orange label.
notes.choices:
A) The division number and compatibility group letter, 1.3C, on an orange label
B) Nothing; the asterisks are printed as shown
C) The identification number of the explosive
D) The compatibility group letter only, on a red label
notes.choicesExplained: B: The asterisks are placeholders that must be replaced. C: The space is for the division number and compatibility group, not an identification number. D: The division number is also needed, and the background is orange.
notes.explanation: For Divisions 1.1 to 1.3 the "**" is replaced with the division number and the compatibility group letter.
notes.source: 49 CFR Part 172 (Revised as of October 1, 2025), § 172.411(b), PDF p. 273
notes.evidence: (b) In addition to complying with § 172.407, the background color on the EXPLOSIVE 1.1, EXPLOSIVE 1.2 and EXPLOSIVE 1.3 labels must be orange. The ‘‘**’’ must be replaced with the appropriate division number and compatibility group letter.

notes.front: Who must label a non-bulk package of a hazardous material, and with which labels?
notes.back: Each person who offers it for transportation or transports it, with the labels specified in the Hazardous Materials Table and subpart E.
notes.explanation: Section 172.400(a) puts the duty on both offerors and transporters, subject to the exceptions in § 172.400a.
notes.source: 49 CFR Part 172 (Revised as of October 1, 2025), § 172.400(a), PDF p. 265
notes.evidence: (a) Except as specified in § 172.400a, each person who offers for transportation or transports a hazardous material in any of the following packages or containment devices, shall label the package or containment device with labels specified for the material in the § 172.101 table and in this subpart: (1) A non-bulk package;

notes.front: Which bulk packagings must be labelled when they are not placarded?
notes.back: Those under 18 m³ (640 cubic feet) other than cargo tanks, portable tanks and tank cars; and portable tanks under 3,785 L (1,000 gallons).
notes.explanation: Section 172.400(a)(2) and (3) list both kinds, and each is excused from labels only when it is placarded under subpart F.
notes.source: 49 CFR Part 172 (Revised as of October 1, 2025), § 172.400(a)(2)–(3), PDF p. 265
notes.evidence: (2) A bulk packaging, other than a cargo tank, portable tank, or tank car, with a volumetric capacity of less than 18 m3 (640 cubic feet), unless placarded in accordance with subpart F of this part; (3) A portable tank of less than 3785 L (1000 gallons) capacity, unless placarded in accordance with subpart F of this part;

notes.front: A shipper sends one 4-litre can of a fully regulated flammable liquid by truck. The driver says no label is needed because the truck will be placarded. Who is right?
notes.back: B: The shipper must label the can; placarding does not remove labels from a non-bulk package.
notes.choices:
A) The driver; placarding replaces labels
B) The shipper must label the can; placarding does not remove labels from a non-bulk package
C) Neither; labels are needed only for air transport
D) The driver; only bulk packagings are labelled
notes.choicesExplained: A: The placarding exception applies to some bulk packagings, not non-bulk packages. C: The rule applies to every mode. D: Non-bulk packages are the first item on the list.
notes.explanation: Section 172.400(a)(1) lists non-bulk packages without any placarding exception.
notes.source: 49 CFR Part 172 (Revised as of October 1, 2025), § 172.400(a), PDF p. 265
notes.evidence: (a) Except as specified in § 172.400a, each person who offers for transportation or transports a hazardous material in any of the following packages or containment devices, shall label the package or containment device with labels specified for the material in the § 172.101 table and in this subpart: (1) A non-bulk package;

notes.front: Which labels must a package of a hazardous material carry under § 172.402(a)?
notes.back: Primary and subsidiary hazard labels as specified in column 6 of the Hazardous Materials Table, unless excepted.
notes.explanation: Column 6 is the starting point; paragraph (a)(2) adds further rules for materials other than Class 1 or Class 2.
notes.source: 49 CFR Part 172 (Revised as of October 1, 2025), § 172.402(a)(1), PDF p. 267
notes.evidence: (1) Shall be labeled with primary and subsidiary hazard labels as specified in column 6 of the § 172.101 table (unless excepted in paragraph (a)(2) of this section); and (2)For other than Class 1 or Class 2 materials

notes.front: Where is the hazard class or division number shown on a label?
notes.back: In the lower corner, on both primary and subsidiary hazard labels.
notes.explanation: The same rule applies to both kinds of label.
notes.source: 49 CFR Part 172 (Revised as of October 1, 2025), § 172.402(b), PDF p. 267
notes.evidence: (b) Display of hazard class on labels. The appropriate hazard class or division number must be displayed in the lower corner of a primary hazard label and a subsidiary hazard label.

notes.front: When is a Division 6.1 subsidiary label not needed on a Class 8 package?
notes.back: When the material’s toxicity comes solely from corrosive destruction of tissue, not systemic poisoning.
notes.explanation: The test is whether the toxicity is systemic or comes only from corrosive destruction of tissue.
notes.source: 49 CFR Part 172 (Revised as of October 1, 2025), § 172.400a(c), PDF p. 266
notes.evidence: a Division 6.1 subsidiary hazard label is not required on a package containing a Class 8 (corrosive) material which has a subsidiary hazard of Division 6.1 (poisonous) if the toxicity of the material is based solely on the corrosive destruction of tissue rather than systemic poisoning.

notes.front: Column 6 of the Hazardous Materials Table shows the codes 3 and 8 for a liquid. Which labels go on its drum?
notes.back: C: FLAMMABLE LIQUID as the primary label and CORROSIVE as the subsidiary, each with its class number.
notes.choices:
A) Only FLAMMABLE LIQUID, since the primary hazard decides
B) Only CORROSIVE, since it is the more serious hazard
C) FLAMMABLE LIQUID as the primary label and CORROSIVE as the subsidiary, each with its class number
D) CORROSIVE as the primary label and FLAMMABLE LIQUID as the subsidiary
notes.choicesExplained: A: Subsidiary labels in column 6 are required too. B: The primary label cannot be dropped. D: The first code in column 6 is the primary hazard.
notes.explanation: Section 172.402(a)(1) requires both the primary and the subsidiary labels that column 6 specifies.
notes.source: 49 CFR Part 172 (Revised as of October 1, 2025), § 172.402(a)(1), PDF p. 267
notes.evidence: (1) Shall be labeled with primary and subsidiary hazard labels as specified in column 6 of the § 172.101 table

notes.front: Which label does a material classed as a combustible liquid need?
notes.back: None. No label is required for a combustible liquid, or for a Class 3 material reclassed as one.
notes.explanation: The exclusion also covers Class 3 materials that have been reclassed as combustible liquids.
notes.source: 49 CFR Part 172 (Revised as of October 1, 2025), § 172.101(g), PDF p. 7
notes.evidence: No label is required for a material classed as a combustible liquid or for a Class 3 material that is reclassed as a combustible liquid.

notes.front: A shipper lawfully reclasses a Class 3 fuel as a combustible liquid and ships it in drums. What label do the drums need?
notes.back: B: No label.
notes.choices:
A) FLAMMABLE LIQUID
B) No label
C) CLASS 9
D) FLAMMABLE LIQUID with the word COMBUSTIBLE added
notes.choicesExplained: A: The material is no longer a Class 3 flammable liquid. C: Combustible liquids are not Class 9. D: No such label modification exists.
notes.explanation: Section 172.101(g) removes the label requirement for combustible liquids, including reclassed Class 3 materials.
notes.source: 49 CFR Part 172 (Revised as of October 1, 2025), § 172.101(g), PDF p. 7
notes.evidence: No label is required for a material classed as a combustible liquid or for a Class 3 material that is reclassed as a combustible liquid.

notes.front: Where on a package must a label be placed?
notes.back: On a surface other than the bottom, and near the proper shipping name marking on the same surface if the package is big enough.
notes.explanation: Section 172.406(a) sets both conditions for every required label, subject to its exceptions.
notes.source: 49 CFR Part 172 (Revised as of October 1, 2025), § 172.406(a)(1), PDF p. 270
notes.evidence: (i) Be printed on or affixed to a surface (other than the bottom) of the package or containment device containing the hazardous material; (ii) Be located on the same surface of the package and near the proper shipping name marking, if the package dimensions are adequate; and

notes.front: What size rule applies to a label on a cylindrical package?
notes.back: The label must be of such dimensions that it will not overlap itself.
notes.explanation: For radioactive cylindrical packages needing two labels, they go on opposite points of the circumference.
notes.source: 49 CFR Part 172 (Revised as of October 1, 2025), § 172.406(a)(1), PDF p. 271
notes.evidence: For cylindrical packages, the label must be of such dimensions that it will not overlap itself. In the case of cylindrical packages containing radioactive materials, which require two identical labels, these labels must be centered on opposite points of the circumference

notes.front: When may a label be printed on or placed on a securely affixed tag instead of the package?
notes.back: For a non-radioactive package smaller than the label, a cylinder, or a package too irregular for a label to be affixed.
notes.explanation: These are the three exceptions in § 172.406(b).
notes.source: 49 CFR Part 172 (Revised as of October 1, 2025), § 172.406(b), PDF p. 271
notes.evidence: (b) Exceptions. A label may be printed on or placed on a securely affixed tag, or may be affixed by other suitable means to: (1) A package that contains no radioactive material and which has dimensions less than those of the required label; (2) A cylinder; and (3) A package which has such an irregular surface

notes.front: A packer puts the OXIDIZER label on the bottom of a large carton, because the sides are covered in printed product information. What is wrong?
notes.back: D: Labels may not go on the bottom; it belongs on another surface, near the proper shipping name marking.
notes.choices:
A) The label should be on a tag instead
B) Nothing, if the carton is stacked label side up
C) Labels must always go on the lid
D) Labels may not go on the bottom; it belongs on another surface, near the proper shipping name marking
notes.choicesExplained: A: Tags are for small, cylindrical or irregular packages. B: The bottom is excluded however the carton is stacked. C: No lid rule exists; any surface other than the bottom may do.
notes.explanation: The bottom is expressly excluded, and the carton is big enough for a label beside the marking.
notes.source: 49 CFR Part 172 (Revised as of October 1, 2025), § 172.406(a)(1), PDF p. 270
notes.evidence: (i) Be printed on or affixed to a surface (other than the bottom) of the package or containment device containing the hazardous material; (ii) Be located on the same surface of the package and near the proper shipping name marking, if the package dimensions are adequate; and

notes.front: How close together must primary and subsidiary hazard labels be?
notes.back: Next to each other; within 150 mm (6 inches) of one another conforms.
notes.explanation: The 150 mm figure is the test for "next to each other" in § 172.406(c).
notes.source: 49 CFR Part 172 (Revised as of October 1, 2025), § 172.406(c), PDF p. 271
notes.evidence: (c) Placement of multiple labels. When primary and subsidiary hazard labels are required, they must be displayed next to each other. Placement conforms to this requirement if labels are within 150 mm (6 inches) of one another.

notes.front: On a drum, the FLAMMABLE LIQUID label is on one side and the CORROSIVE subsidiary label is on the opposite side, about 500 mm away. Does this conform?
notes.back: B: No; the labels must be next to each other, within 150 mm.
notes.choices:
A) Yes; any two sides are acceptable
B) No; the labels must be next to each other, within 150 mm
C) Yes, if both labels are the full 100 mm
D) No; the subsidiary label must go on the bottom
notes.choicesExplained: A: The labels must be next to each other. C: Size does not change the placement rule. D: Labels may never go on the bottom.
notes.explanation: At 500 mm apart, the labels are not next to each other as § 172.406(c) requires.
notes.source: 49 CFR Part 172 (Revised as of October 1, 2025), § 172.406(c), PDF p. 271
notes.evidence: When primary and subsidiary hazard labels are required, they must be displayed next to each other. Placement conforms to this requirement if labels are within 150 mm (6 inches) of one another.

notes.front: What must a label be placed on, or have, so that it is visible?
notes.back: A background of contrasting colour, or a dotted or solid line outer border.
notes.explanation: The border may also be used on a contrasting background.
notes.source: 49 CFR Part 172 (Revised as of October 1, 2025), § 172.406(d), PDF p. 271
notes.evidence: (d) Contrast with background. Each label must be printed on or affixed to a background color contrasting to the color specification of the label as required by § 172.407(d)(1), or must have a dotted or solid line outer border, to enhance the visibility of the label.

notes.front: Which packages must show duplicate labels on at least two sides or two ends, other than the bottom?
notes.back: Among others: packages or overpacks of 1.8 m³ (64 cubic feet) or more, and non-bulk packages of radioactive material.
notes.explanation: Generally only one of each required label is needed; these are exceptions to that.
notes.source: 49 CFR Part 172 (Revised as of October 1, 2025), § 172.406(e), PDF p. 271
notes.evidence: Generally, only one of each different required label must be displayed on a package. However, duplicate labels must be displayed on at least two sides or two ends (other than the bottom) of— (1) Each package or overpack having a volume of 1.8 m 3 (64 cubic feet) or more; (2) Each non-bulk package containing a radioactive material;

notes.front: What is the minimum size of a diamond (square-on-point) label?
notes.back: At least 100 mm (3.9 inches) on each side, with a solid inner border about 5 mm inside the edge.
notes.explanation: The 5 mm is measured from the outside edge of the label to the outside of the inner border line.
notes.source: 49 CFR Part 172 (Revised as of October 1, 2025), § 172.407(c)(1), PDF p. 271
notes.evidence: (1) Each diamond (square-onpoint) label prescribed in this subpart must be at least 100 mm (3.9 inches) on each side with each side having a solid line inner border approximately 5 mm (.2 inches) inside and parallel to the edge.

notes.front: May a label be made smaller than 100 mm?
notes.back: Yes, if the package's size requires it: its dimensions and features may be reduced proportionally, keeping the symbol and other elements clearly visible.
notes.explanation: The reduction is allowed only because the package is too small for a full-size label, and every element must stay clearly visible.
notes.source: 49 CFR Part 172 (Revised as of October 1, 2025), § 172.407(c)(1)(i), PDF p. 272
notes.evidence: its features may be reduced proportionally provided the symbol and other elements of the label remain clearly visible.

notes.front: May a packaging labelled before 1 January 2017 to the earlier label rules stay in domestic service?
notes.back: Yes, until the end of its useful life, if it met the requirements in effect on 31 December 2014.
notes.explanation: This transitional rule covers domestic transportation only.
notes.source: 49 CFR Part 172 (Revised as of October 1, 2025), § 172.407(c)(1)(iv), PDF p. 272
notes.evidence: (iv) For domestic transportation, a packaging labeled prior to January 1, 2017, and in conformance with the requirements of this paragraph in effect on December 31, 2014, may continue in service until the end of its useful life.

notes.front: How high must the class or division number on a label be?
notes.back: At least 6.3 mm (0.25 inches) and not more than 12.7 mm (0.5 inches), unless the subpart says otherwise.
notes.explanation: The number has both a minimum and a maximum height.
notes.source: 49 CFR Part 172 (Revised as of October 1, 2025), § 172.407(c)(3), PDF p. 272
notes.evidence: (3) Except as otherwise provided in this subpart, the hazard class number, or division number, as appropriate, must be at least 6.3 mm (0.25 inches) and not greater than 12.7 mm (0.5 inches).

notes.front: Must a primary or subsidiary label for Classes 1 to 6 or 8 carry words describing the hazard?
notes.back: No. For Classes 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6 and 8, text indicating the hazard is not required.
notes.explanation: The rule covers primary and subsidiary labels for the listed classes; Classes 7 and 9 are not listed.
notes.source: 49 CFR Part 172 (Revised as of October 1, 2025), § 172.405(a), PDF p. 270
notes.evidence: (a) For Classes 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, and 8, text indicating a hazard (for example FLAMMABLE LIQUID) is not required on a primary or subsidiary label.

notes.front: What exposure must a label withstand without deteriorating or substantially changing colour?
notes.back: A 30-day exposure to conditions reasonably expected in transportation.
notes.explanation: Every label, printed or affixed, must be durable and weather resistant.
notes.source: 49 CFR Part 172 (Revised as of October 1, 2025), § 172.407(a), PDF p. 271
notes.evidence: (a) Durability. Each label, whether printed on or affixed to a package, must be durable and weather resistant. A label on a package must be able to withstand, without deterioration or a substantial change in color, a 30-day exposure to conditions incident to transportation that reasonably could be expected to be encountered by the labeled package.

notes.front: May a label made to the UN Recommendations or other listed international rules replace the matching label in this subpart?
notes.back: Yes, except for materials poisonous by inhalation.
notes.explanation: Section 172.407(f) lists the UN Recommendations and other international codes as acceptable label specifications.
notes.source: 49 CFR Part 172 (Revised as of October 1, 2025), § 172.407(f), PDF p. 273
notes.evidence: (f) Exceptions. Except for materials poisonous by inhalation (see § 171.8 of this subchapter), a label conforming to specifications in the UN Recommendations, the ICAO Technical Instructions, the IMDG Code, or the Transport Canada TDG Regulations (IBR, see § 171.7 of this subchapter) may be used in place of a corresponding label

notes.front: A 60 mm-tall bottle of a Division 6.1 liquid is shipped alone in no outer packaging and cannot take a 100 mm label. What may the shipper do?
notes.back: D: Reduce the label proportionally, keeping the symbol and other elements clearly visible.
notes.choices:
A) Leave the label off
B) Print only the class number
C) Use a 100 mm label folded round the bottle
D) Reduce the label proportionally, keeping the symbol and other elements clearly visible
notes.choicesExplained: A: The label is still required. B: The symbol and other elements must remain. C: Folding would hide parts of the label and let it overlap.
notes.explanation: The package size requires a smaller label, and § 172.407(c)(1)(i) allows proportional reduction.
notes.source: 49 CFR Part 172 (Revised as of October 1, 2025), § 172.407(c)(1)(i), PDF p. 272
notes.evidence: its features may be reduced proportionally provided the symbol and other elements of the label remain clearly visible.

notes.front: When may a package bear a hazard label, as a general rule?
notes.back: Only when it contains a hazardous material and the label represents a hazard of that material.
notes.explanation: Both conditions must be met: hazardous contents, and a label that matches their hazard.
notes.source: 49 CFR Part 172 (Revised as of October 1, 2025), § 172.401(a), PDF p. 267
notes.evidence: (1) The package contains a material that is a hazardous material, and (2) The label represents a hazard of the hazardous material in the package.

notes.front: May a package carry a marking or label that could be confused with a hazard label?
notes.back: No, if its colour, design or shape could be confused or conflict with a prescribed label.
notes.explanation: The ban binds both the person offering the package and the carrier transporting it.
notes.source: 49 CFR Part 172 (Revised as of October 1, 2025), § 172.401(b)–(c), PDF p. 267
notes.evidence: (b) No person may offer for transportation and no carrier may transport a package bearing any marking or label which by its color, design, or shape could be confused with or conflict with a label prescribed by this part.

notes.front: How is an overpack labelled when it holds compatible hazardous materials of different classes?
notes.back: With the labels required for each class inside, unless labels representing each hazardous material inside are visible.
notes.explanation: This is the consolidated packaging rule of § 172.404(b).
notes.source: 49 CFR Part 172 (Revised as of October 1, 2025), § 172.404(b), PDF p. 270
notes.evidence: (b) Consolidated packaging. When two or more packages containing compatible hazardous materials are placed within the same outside container or overpack, the outside container or overpack must be labeled as required for each class of hazardous material contained therein, unless labels representative of each hazardous material in the outside container or overpack are visible.

notes.front: When must a package carry the CARGO AIRCRAFT ONLY label?
notes.back: When it goes by aircraft and contains a hazardous material authorised on cargo aircraft only.
notes.explanation: The trigger is air transport of a material authorised on cargo aircraft only.
notes.source: 49 CFR Part 172 (Revised as of October 1, 2025), § 172.402(c), PDF p. 267
notes.evidence: (c) Cargo Aircraft Only label. Each person who offers for transportation or transports by aircraft a package containing a hazardous material which is authorized on cargo aircraft only shall label the package with a CARGO AIRCRAFT ONLY label specified in § 172.448 of this subpart.

notes.front: What size must the CARGO AIRCRAFT ONLY label be?
notes.back: A rectangle at least 110 mm high by 120 mm wide, with the words in letters at least 6.3 mm high.
notes.explanation: Unlike the hazard labels, it is a rectangle, not a diamond.
notes.source: 49 CFR Part 172 (Revised as of October 1, 2025), § 172.407(c)(2), PDF p. 272
notes.evidence: (2) The CARGO AIRCRAFT ONLY label must be a rectangle measuring at least 110 mm (4.3 inches) in height by 120 mm (4.7 inches) in width. The words ‘‘CARGO AIRCRAFT ONLY’’ must be shown in letters measuring at least 6.3 mm (0.25 inches) in height.

notes.front: A package of a flammable liquid in a quantity authorised only on cargo aircraft is booked on a freight flight. Which labels does it need?
notes.back: B: FLAMMABLE LIQUID and CARGO AIRCRAFT ONLY.
notes.choices:
A) CARGO AIRCRAFT ONLY only
B) FLAMMABLE LIQUID and CARGO AIRCRAFT ONLY
C) FLAMMABLE LIQUID only, since the flight carries no passengers
D) No labels; air waybills replace them
notes.choicesExplained: A: The hazard label cannot be dropped. C: The rule applies to cargo-aircraft-only materials whatever the flight. D: Labels are required on the package.
notes.explanation: The hazard label is still needed; § 172.402(c) adds the CARGO AIRCRAFT ONLY label.
notes.source: 49 CFR Part 172 (Revised as of October 1, 2025), § 172.402(c), PDF p. 267
notes.evidence: Each person who offers for transportation or transports by aircraft a package containing a hazardous material which is authorized on cargo aircraft only shall label the package with a CARGO AIRCRAFT ONLY label

notes.front: How many RADIOACTIVE labels must a package of radioactive material carry, and where?
notes.back: Two, affixed to opposite sides of the package.
notes.explanation: Section 172.403(f) applies to every package that must bear a RADIOACTIVE label.
notes.source: 49 CFR Part 172 (Revised as of October 1, 2025), § 172.403(f), PDF p. 269
notes.evidence: (f) Each package required by this section to be labeled with a RADIOACTIVE label must have two of these labels, affixed to opposite sides of the package.

notes.front: How is the category of RADIOACTIVE label chosen when two determining conditions point to different labels?
notes.back: The highest category required by either condition applies.
notes.explanation: The two conditions are the radiation level at the package surface and the transport index.
notes.source: 49 CFR Part 172 (Revised as of October 1, 2025), § 172.403(b), PDF p. 268
notes.evidence: based on the radiation level at the surface of the package and the transport index. The proper category of label must be determined in accordance with paragraph (c) of this section. The label to be applied must be the highest category required for any of the two determining conditions for the package.

notes.front: A package’s transport index calls for a RADIOACTIVE YELLOW-II label, but its surface radiation level calls for RADIOACTIVE YELLOW-III. Which label does it get?
notes.back: C: RADIOACTIVE YELLOW-III.
notes.choices:
A) RADIOACTIVE YELLOW-II
B) Both labels, one of each
C) RADIOACTIVE YELLOW-III
D) RADIOACTIVE WHITE-I, as the default
notes.choicesExplained: A: The lower category does not apply. B: Only the highest category is applied. D: WHITE-I is the lowest category.
notes.explanation: The highest category required by either condition applies.
notes.source: 49 CFR Part 172 (Revised as of October 1, 2025), § 172.403(b), PDF p. 268
notes.evidence: The label to be applied must be the highest category required for any of the two determining conditions for the package. RADIOACTIVE WHITE-I is the lowest category and RADIOACTIVE YELLOW-III is the highest.

notes.front: What is the order of the three RADIOACTIVE labels, from lowest to highest category?
notes.back: RADIOACTIVE WHITE-I (lowest), RADIOACTIVE YELLOW-II, RADIOACTIVE YELLOW-III (highest).
notes.explanation: When two conditions point to different labels, the highest category applies.
notes.source: 49 CFR Part 172 (Revised as of October 1, 2025), § 172.403(b), PDF p. 268
notes.evidence: The label to be applied must be the highest category required for any of the two determining conditions for the package. RADIOACTIVE WHITE-I is the lowest category and RADIOACTIVE YELLOW-III is the highest.

notes.front: A package holds a Division 4.3 material. Which label is its primary label?
notes.back: D: DANGEROUS WHEN WET.
notes.choices:
A) FLAMMABLE SOLID
B) SPONTANEOUSLY COMBUSTIBLE
C) OXIDIZER
D) DANGEROUS WHEN WET
notes.choicesExplained: A: FLAMMABLE SOLID is Division 4.1. B: SPONTANEOUSLY COMBUSTIBLE is Division 4.2. C: OXIDIZER is Division 5.1.
notes.explanation: The DANGEROUS WHEN WET label is the blue Class 4 label.
notes.source: 49 CFR Part 172 (Revised as of October 1, 2025), § 172.423(b), PDF p. 276
notes.evidence: (b) In addition to complying with § 172.407, the background color on the DANGEROUS WHEN WET label must be blue.

notes.front: A drum holds a Division 5.2 material. Which label is its primary label?
notes.back: C: ORGANIC PEROXIDE.
notes.choices:
A) OXIDIZER
B) FLAMMABLE LIQUID
C) ORGANIC PEROXIDE
D) SPONTANEOUSLY COMBUSTIBLE
notes.choicesExplained: A: OXIDIZER is Division 5.1. B: FLAMMABLE LIQUID is Class 3. D: SPONTANEOUSLY COMBUSTIBLE is Division 4.2.
notes.explanation: The ORGANIC PEROXIDE label, red over yellow, carries the number 5.2.
notes.source: 49 CFR Part 172 (Revised as of October 1, 2025), § 172.427(b), PDF p. 278
notes.evidence: (b) In addition to complying with § 172.407, the background on the ORGANIC PEROXIDE label must be red in the top half and yellow in the lower half.

notes.front: A cylinder of a Division 2.2 gas is shipped. Which label does it take as its primary label?
notes.back: D: NON-FLAMMABLE GAS.
notes.choices:
A) OXIDIZER
B) FLAMMABLE GAS
C) POISON GAS
D) NON-FLAMMABLE GAS
notes.choicesExplained: A: OXIDIZER is Division 5.1. B: FLAMMABLE GAS is Division 2.1. C: POISON GAS is Division 2.3.
notes.explanation: The NON-FLAMMABLE GAS label is the green Class 2 label.
notes.source: 49 CFR Part 172 (Revised as of October 1, 2025), § 172.415(b), PDF p. 275
notes.evidence: NON-FLAMMABLE GAS label must be green.

notes.front: A Division 6.1 liquid is poisonous by inhalation, in Hazard Zone A. Which label does it take as its primary label?
notes.back: C: POISON INHALATION HAZARD.
notes.choices:
A) POISON
B) CORROSIVE
C) POISON INHALATION HAZARD
D) INFECTIOUS SUBSTANCE
notes.choicesExplained: A: POISON is for Division 6.1 materials other than inhalation hazards in Zone A or B. B: CORROSIVE is Class 8. D: INFECTIOUS SUBSTANCE is Division 6.2.
notes.explanation: This is the Class 6 label with the black upper diamond, the same scheme as POISON GAS.
notes.source: 49 CFR Part 172 (Revised as of October 1, 2025), § 172.429(b), PDF p. 278
notes.evidence: (b) In addition to complying with § 172.407, the background on the POISON INHALATION HAZARD label and the symbol must be white. The background of the upper diamond must be black

notes.front: A carton holds bottles of a Class 8 material. Which label is its primary label?
notes.back: A: CORROSIVE.
notes.choices:
A) CORROSIVE
B) POISON
C) OXIDIZER
D) CLASS 9
notes.choicesExplained: B: POISON is Division 6.1. C: OXIDIZER is Division 5.1. D: CLASS 9 is for miscellaneous hazardous materials.
notes.explanation: The CORROSIVE label is white over black, with white text and class number 8.
notes.source: 49 CFR Part 172 (Revised as of October 1, 2025), § 172.442(b), PDF p. 281
notes.evidence: (b) In addition to complying with § 172.407, the background on the CORROSIVE label must be white in the top half and black in the lower half.

notes.front: A drum holds a Division 4.2 material. Which label is its primary label?
notes.back: D: SPONTANEOUSLY COMBUSTIBLE.
notes.choices:
A) FLAMMABLE SOLID
B) FLAMMABLE GAS
C) DANGEROUS WHEN WET
D) SPONTANEOUSLY COMBUSTIBLE
notes.choicesExplained: A: FLAMMABLE SOLID is Division 4.1. B: FLAMMABLE GAS is Division 2.1. C: DANGEROUS WHEN WET is Division 4.3.
notes.explanation: The SPONTANEOUSLY COMBUSTIBLE label is white over red, numbered 4.
notes.source: 49 CFR Part 172 (Revised as of October 1, 2025), § 172.422(b), PDF p. 276
notes.evidence: (b) In addition to complying with § 172.407, the background color on the lower half of the SPONTANEOUSLY COMBUSTIBLE label must be red and the upper half must be white.

notes.front: Within Division 6.1, which materials take the POISON INHALATION HAZARD label rather than the POISON label?
notes.back: Materials poisonous by inhalation; the POISON label is for Division 6.1 materials other than those.
notes.explanation: The two labels differ visibly: the inhalation label has a black upper diamond.
notes.source: 49 CFR Part 172 (Revised as of October 1, 2025), § 172.429(b), PDF p. 278
notes.evidence: the background on the POISON INHALATION HAZARD label and the symbol must be white. The background of the upper diamond must be black

notes.front: The FLAMMABLE GAS and FLAMMABLE LIQUID labels are both red with a flame. What tells them apart?
notes.back: The class number: 2 on the FLAMMABLE GAS label, 3 on the FLAMMABLE LIQUID label (and the words, when used).
notes.explanation: The class or division number must appear in the lower corner of every primary and subsidiary label.
notes.source: 49 CFR Part 172 (Revised as of October 1, 2025), § 172.402(b), PDF p. 267
notes.evidence: (b) Display of hazard class on labels. The appropriate hazard class or division number must be displayed in the lower corner of a primary hazard label and a subsidiary hazard label.

notes.front: What word may replace POISON on the POISON label?
notes.back: `TOXIC`.
notes.explanation: Section 172.430(b) allows either word on the white Division 6.1 label.
notes.source: 49 CFR Part 172 (Revised as of October 1, 2025), § 172.430(b), PDF p. 278
notes.evidence: The word ‘‘TOXIC’’ may be used in lieu of the word ‘‘POISON’’.
